chapters.title: Chapter 5: Matching the Method to the Business

lessons.title: Valuing High-Growth and Loss-Making Companies: New-Age Tech Listings

children.text: Between 2021 and 2022 a wave of Indian technology companies listed on NSE and BSE: food delivery, payments, beauty retail, logistics, insurance distribution. Almost all of them were loss-making. Their P/E ratios did not exist, their book values meant little, and many fell sharply in the months after listing before some found their footing. Investors were left asking a fair question: how do you value a company that has never made a profit?

body.text: A loss-making company is not unvaluable. It is a bet on a future steady state. Describe that state explicitly, how large the revenue, how profitable the margin, how much capital it needs, then discount it back and weight it against the chance of failure.

children.text: Why the Usual Tools Go Quiet

body.caption: What breaks when there are no profits

cells: Undefined with negative earnings; meaningless in the first profitable year, when the multiple looks absurd
EBITDA is negative, and "adjusted EBITDA" often excludes real costs such as employee stock options
The valuable assets are brand, network, technology and customer habits, which are not on the balance sheet
Works arithmetically, but silently assumes a mature margin. Chapter 4 showed how much it can hide.
The listed peer set is small, recently listed and often loss-making too, so everyone anchors on everyone else

body.text: Watch the vocabulary in these companies' disclosures. Gross order value or gross merchandise value is the value of goods sold through the platform, not the company's revenue. Revenue is the commission, delivery and advertising income it keeps. "Adjusted EBITDA before ESOP cost" removes a genuine cost of employing people. When a company reports "contribution margin positive", ask which costs sit below that line.

children.text: Framework 1: Value the Steady State, Then Discount Back
The most reliable approach is to stop asking what the company earns today and start describing what it will look like when it matures. Four questions do most of the work.
How big can revenue get?
Build it from market size and a defensible share, or from users, frequency and spend per user.
What margin will a mature version of this business earn?
Look at mature analogues in India and abroad, allowing for how competitive the category is.
How much capital does that growth need?
Use a sales-to-capital ratio, which is high for asset-light platforms.
What could go wrong?
Set an explicit probability of failure and a value in that case, usually little more than remaining cash.
Worked example: QuickBasket

QuickBasket is a fictional NSE-listed quick-commerce platform. Revenue last year was ₹8,000 crore with an EBIT margin of -8.0%, so it lost money. It holds ₹3,000 crore of cash, has no debt, 90 crore shares outstanding and 97 crore on a fully diluted basis after employee stock options. The shares trade at ₹180.

The base case assumes revenue growth fading from 40.0% in year 1 to 9.0% by year 10, and the EBIT margin improving in a straight line from -8.0% to 10.0%, a level consistent with a mature, competitive retail platform. Capital is added at ₹1 for every ₹4 of new revenue, the cost of capital is 12.0% reflecting high risk, and beyond year 10 the business grows at 6.0% earning 18.0% on new capital. No tax benefit is assumed for the loss years, which is conservative.

body.title: QuickBasket base case: revenue and EBIT margin path

body.text: Notice how lopsided the value is: 129.8% of enterprise value sits in the terminal value, because the early years consume cash rather than produce it. For loss-making companies, almost everything depends on assumptions about a business that does not yet exist. That is not a reason to avoid the exercise. It is a reason to run scenarios rather than a single number.

children.text: Scenarios and the Probability of Failure
One path is never enough here. Build a small number of complete stories, then weight them. Crucially, include the possibility that the company never gets there.

cells: Competition keeps discounts high; margins barely turn positive
Scale brings advertising income and better delivery density
Market consolidates to two players with real pricing power

body.caption: Probability-weighted scenarios, then adjusted for the chance of failure

stats.label: Probability of failure
stats.context: Value in that case: ₹20.6 per share, roughly remaining cash

stats.label: Dilution drag
stats.context: Value per share lost to employee stock options alone

children.text: At ₹180, the market is paying more than this framework suggests, which means it is assigning a higher probability to the bull case, expecting a larger mature margin, or requiring a lower return than the 12.0% used here. A reverse DCF, as in Chapter 3, turns that into a single testable question: what mature margin and market size does ₹180 require?

body.text: Dilution is not a detail for these companies. Large employee stock option pools, and future equity raises to fund losses, both reduce your share of whatever value is eventually created. Always value on a fully diluted basis, and if the company will need more capital before turning cash positive, model that raise explicitly.

children.text: Framework 2: Unit Economics
A ten-year forecast is only credible if the underlying
unit economics
can work. For a delivery platform, the unit is an order.

markDefs.definition: The revenue and costs associated with a single unit of business, such as one order or one customer. They reveal whether a business becomes profitable as it grows, or simply loses money faster.

cells: What the customer pays for goods
A take rate of 40.0%: commissions, delivery fees and advertising
After delivery, packaging, discounts and payment costs
Technology, dark stores, corporate overheads, marketing
20.0% more orders needed at today's contribution margin

children.text: This single table tells you more than any multiple. At ₹25 of contribution per order, QuickBasket needs 20.0% more orders just to cover fixed costs. It can get there by growing orders, by raising the contribution margin through higher fees, advertising income or lower delivery cost per order, or both. If neither is realistic, no DCF assumption about year 10 margins is credible.
The customer view: LTV against CAC

body.caption: A simple lifetime value estimate and how long it takes to recover the cost of acquiring a customer

stats.label: Customer acquisition cost
stats.context: Discounts and marketing to win one customer

stats.label: LTV to CAC
stats.context: Payback in 2.0 years; investors usually look for 3× or better

children.text: At 1.67 times, QuickBasket's customers are barely worth more than the cost of acquiring them, so spending to grow destroys value rather than creating it. The bull case depends on this improving: at ₹45 of contribution per order and 18 orders a year, the ratio rises to 4.50 times. When you read a new-age company's earnings call, this is the transition management is really describing when it talks about a path to profitability.
A Checklist for New-Age Listings

body.title: Before valuing a loss-making platform
steps: Separate gross order value from revenue, and understand the take rate.
Find contribution margin per order or per customer, and what costs sit below that line.
Check whether "adjusted EBITDA" excludes employee stock option costs, and add them back.
Work out fixed costs and the volume needed to cover them at current contribution margins.
Check LTV against CAC and the payback period, and whether retention is disclosed by cohort.
Count fully diluted shares, including the unvested ESOP pool.
Estimate how long the cash lasts at the current burn rate, and whether another equity raise is needed.
Write down a mature revenue and margin, justify them with a comparable business, and only then build the DCF.
Assign an explicit probability of failure and a value in that case.

children.text: Check Your Understanding

body.title: Orders needed to break even
body.prompt: A food delivery platform earns a contribution margin of ₹30 per order and has annual fixed costs of ₹900 crore. How many orders a year, in crore, does it need to break even at the operating level?
body.explanation: ₹900 crore ÷ ₹30 per order = 30 crore orders a year, about 8.2 lakh orders a day. Growth alone fixes the problem only if contribution margin per order stays positive as the platform expands into smaller cities.

body.title: LTV to CAC
body.prompt: A subscription app earns ₹40 of contribution per month from each customer, retains 65% of customers each year and spends ₹400 to acquire one. What is its LTV to CAC ratio? Answer to two decimal places.
body.explanation: Annual contribution = ₹40 × 12 = ₹480. LTV = ₹480 ÷ (1 - 0.65) = ₹1,371. LTV ÷ CAC = ₹1,371 ÷ ₹400 = 3.43×, comfortably above the 3× level investors usually look for.

body.title: What an EV/Sales multiple assumes
body.question: A loss-making logistics platform trades at 6 times sales. A comparable mature listed logistics company trades at 1.5 times sales with a 9% EBIT margin. What does the 6 times multiple most likely imply?
options: The platform is four times better managed than the mature company
The market expects its revenue to grow several times over, and its margin to reach at least mature levels, before it settles into a steady state
EV/Sales cannot be compared between companies
The platform will be acquired at a premium
body.explanation: EV/Sales embeds an assumed margin. Paying four times the mature company's sales multiple only makes sense if revenue grows substantially from here, margins reach or exceed mature levels, or both. Converting the multiple into implied revenue and margin, as in Chapter 4, makes the assumption explicit.

body.title: Mind the vocabulary
body.textWithBlank: For a marketplace platform, gross order value is the value of goods sold through the platform, which is not the same as its ___.
body.explanation: Revenue is what the platform keeps: commissions, delivery charges and advertising income. Valuing a platform on a multiple of gross order value confuses the two and inflates the apparent size of the business.

body.title: The GMV multiple pitch
body.scenario: Rohan, an analyst at a Mumbai family office, receives a note on a loss-making online pharmacy. It argues: "The company trades at 0.9 times GMV, against 2.5 times GMV for global e-commerce leaders, so it is undervalued." The company's GMV is ₹9,000 crore, revenue is ₹1,800 crore, contribution margin is 4% of GMV, annual fixed costs are ₹900 crore, and it has ₹1,500 crore of cash, burning ₹500 crore a year. Its ESOP pool is 9% of fully diluted shares.
body.prompt: What is wrong with the pitch, and how should Rohan value the company instead?
body.modelAnswer:
1. GMV is not revenue. With revenue of ₹1,800 crore on ₹9,000 crore of GMV, the take rate is 20%. On revenue, 0.9 times GMV is 4.5 times sales, which is not obviously cheap for a loss-making business.
2. The comparison is not like for like. Global e-commerce leaders have different take rates, category mixes and margins. A GMV multiple can only be compared where the economics are genuinely similar.
3. Unit economics decide the outcome. Contribution is 4% of ₹9,000 crore, or ₹360 crore, against ₹900 crore of fixed costs. GMV would need to roughly two and a half times at the same contribution margin just to cover fixed costs.
4. Cash runway matters. Burning ₹500 crore a year against ₹1,500 crore of cash gives about three years. If profitability is further away than that, a fresh equity raise is coming, and existing shareholders will be diluted, on top of the 9% ESOP pool.
5. The right approach: build a ten-year steady-state model with a mature revenue base, a margin justified by a comparable mature pharmacy or retail business, reinvestment through a sales-to-capital ratio and a high discount rate. Run bear, base and bull scenarios, apply an explicit probability of failure, and value on fully diluted shares. Then use a reverse DCF to see what the current price implies.

points: Loss-making companies can be valued, but only by describing the mature business they are trying to become.
Forecast revenue from market size and share, set a mature margin from comparable businesses, add capital through a sales-to-capital ratio, and discount at a high cost of capital.
Almost all the value sits in the terminal year, so use scenarios rather than a single forecast, and include an explicit probability of failure.
Unit economics decide whether the story is possible: contribution per order, fixed costs, break-even volume, LTV against CAC and payback.
Gross order value is not revenue, and adjusted EBITDA that excludes ESOP costs understates real expenses.
Always value on fully diluted shares, and model future equity raises where the company is still burning cash.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment advice. QuickBasket, the online pharmacy described and the individuals named are fictional, and all figures are illustrative. References to the 2021 and 2022 listing wave are general market history. Consult a SEBI-registered investment adviser before making investment decisions.
